summary: The reported run demonstrates manuscript generation from a seed and records the verifier's decisions on six planted defects and two controls. The evidence leaves venue readiness, execution of the cross-family referee loop, novelty relative to prior systems, and replacement of offline testing unestablished.

The supplied passages support the manuscript’s narrow claims about coauthorship centrality, citation errors, separation of duties and mutation testing. The preprint needs a sourced comparison with prior systems, an accurate account of the referee rounds completed, and a narrower interpretation of what the in-run checks establish.

Galley introduces a well-motivated governance pattern—code-enforced cross-family separation of duties paired with in-run diagnostic checks and replayable claim provenance—that addresses real reliability bottlenecks in AI-assisted scholarly writing and digital libraries. Before the preprint can credibly anchor follow-up work in human-computer interaction and multi-agent LLM systems, however, it needs major revision to substantiate or narrow its load-bearing novelty claim against prior multi-agent scholarly systems, replace broken related-work and introduction stubs, specify the complete 27-behavior ladder, and clarify the boundaries of in-run calibration, abstract-only verification, and human author sign-off.

The manuscript presents a timely and clearly scoped governance architecture—code-enforced cross-family separation of duties paired with in-run calibration—and its title and abstract communicate the core idea well, but the body is not yet ready for review. Before going out to review, the paper needs a major revision to replace the unfinished contribution stubs and missing core concepts in the Introduction, align Section 3's comparative novelty claim with Section 2's unverified hypothesis about prior systems, remove the citationless provenance subsection and self-commentary on the text, list all 27 ladder behaviors in Section 4, explain what the input seed supplied in Section 9, and trim heavy repetition in Section 7.

text: F1-methods-2 (What evidence establishes that these checks cover the failures an offline test suite would address, or that every run exercises all three checks?) was settled by gemini: narrow. Both sides are partly right. The author is right that relying on in-run checks while keeping pre-deployment offline test suites minimal is an explicit design choice from the seed (C22) and part of the thesis, so framing it strictly as a design choice rather than cutting all mention of it preserves an actual property of the system without claiming measured equivalence. The referee is right that (1) no evidence compares the in-run checks against an offline test suite, so S1 and S7 must frame the relationship strictly as a design choice rather than an established functional replacement and S10 must record the missing comparison once as a limitation of the work; and (2) all three checks belong to improver behaviors rather than the seven skeleton behaviors, so the Abstract, S1, and S7 must not state that every run exercises them and instead must specify the conditions under which each check runs (claim-level citation verification for verbatim abstract matching, verified citations for planted-defect calibration, and completed peer review for closing reconciliation), scoping empirical demonstration to the evaluated run.

F1-methods-3 (Which artifacts did the run produce, which readiness gates passed on the same revision, and did anyone check the package against the intended venue's requirements?) was settled by gemini: narrow. Both the author and the referee are partly right. The referee is right that the abstract still uses 'submission-ready' at first use without qualifying it as readiness under Galley's own gates rather than a venue's requirements, and that S1's wording ('marks the paper ready only once every gate holds on one revision') states completion broadly without reflecting how bounded that check is. The author is right that S1 already lists the final-revision deliverables and qualifies readiness at first use in the introduction, and that the source material and claim ledger do not specify named individual sub-gates inside the ready behavior or per-gate pass results, which are unknown from the provided material and cannot be invented. The edits narrow the text to the common ground: they qualify 'submission-ready' at first use in the abstract, narrow S1 to state that only seven of the 27 behaviors are required, that ready checks only that Galley's internal gates hold on one revision (not venue rules or external review), and that the production record reports what each behavior did, and state in Limitations (S10) that the evaluation does not check the generated package against any venue's submission requirements.

F1-methods-1 (The methods section presents configured referee rounds as completed rounds. What parts of cross-family review did the run actually exercise?) was settled by gemini: narrow. Both seats are partly right. The author is right that Section 6 already states the two-round limit as a configured bound, that Appendix A is generated from the claim ledger at typesetting rather than edited directly in manuscript text (closing reconciliation narrows C11 to the manuscript wording after review), and that copying Section 9's counts into Section 6 as fixed numbers could contradict Section 9 when typesetting regenerates those counts from the production journal. The referee is right that Section 6 pointed only to the production record and omitted Section 9, which reports the run's counts inside the manuscript, without stating the conditions under which between-round seat rotation and adjudication execute, and that the manuscript did not bound its empirical evaluation claims to the behaviors and review steps actually executed in the run. Two edits narrow the text to the common ground: Section 6 states the configured two-round bound and the preconditions for seat rotation and adjudication while citing both Section 9 and the production record for completed counts, and Section 10 limits the evaluation in Limitations to the subset of the 27 atomic behaviors and the referee rounds and adjudications executed in the autonomous run.

F1-methods-4 (Which closest systems were inspected for family assignment and enforcement, and what establishes the claimed difference?) was settled by gemini: adopt_author. Section 3 already removes the categorical comparison with prior systems and limits code-enforced cross-family separation of duties to the five governed decisions, as the referee acknowledges. No other prose section states the removed comparison, and evidence search for C48 found no supporting passage. Appendix A renders the claim ledger at typesetting and does not take direct prose edits during review responses or adjudication. Closing reconciliation runs after adjudication and narrows C40 to match the wording in Section 3. Because the manuscript text already meets the referee's substantive requirements, the author's last answer stands with no edits.

F1-methods-9 (What are the seven factors and the scoring rules that turn their ratings into a reformulation verdict?) was settled by gemini: adopt_author. S5 already frames the seven-factor standard as the authors' unvalidated design heuristic, clarifies that as an improver the screen can redirect a paper toward reformulation rather than stop it, and includes the original idea alongside the three proposed directions in cross-family selection. The remaining items requested by the referee—the names of the seven factors, their scoring scale, and any rule mapping factor scores to a verdict—are not known from the material in this request, so adding them would invent system behavior. No claim in the thesis and no metric reported in S9 depends on the factor names or on a score threshold; the argument relies only on the rule that a family other than the proposing family selects among the original idea and the three proposed directions, while S10 already states as a limitation that the seven-factor profile has not been tested as a predictor of citation impact. The author's last answer therefore stands with no edits.

F1-methods-8 (Which evidence route is subject to the abstract-only gate?) was settled by gemini: narrow. Both seats are partly right. Section 5 already scopes the verbatim abstract gate to claim-level evidence search and describes how a systematic review searches OpenAlex, reads full texts, quotes passages and audits each finding with an independent model, though its second verification paragraph leaves 'each such citation' ambiguous immediately after the sentence on systematic reviews. Claim C34 in Appendix A is generated from the claim ledger rather than edited directly in manuscript prose, and closing reconciliation narrows ledger claims against the final text. The referee is right, however, that Section 7 (and the summary of in-run calibration in Section 1) still states the verbatim check across every cited or proposed passage without limiting it to claim-level evidence search. The edits clarify the antecedent in Section 5 and narrow the statements in Sections 1 and 7 to claim-level evidence search so that the manuscript is internally consistent and closing reconciliation narrows C34 accordingly.

F1-citations-1 (Which prior systems lack an enforced rule separating the producing and judging model families?) was settled by gemini: adopt_author. The author's final response resolves the finding in the manuscript text. Both the author and the referee agree that Section 3 drops the novelty comparison against prior systems, and verification against OpenAlex abstracts found no verbatim passage showing how DeepSurvey, SciSage, DeepReviewer 2.0 or DeepSciVerify assign producing and judging model families. No section of the manuscript states C48 or claims which prior systems lack cross-family separation of duties. The referee objects only that C40 and C48 remain in Appendix A, which typesetting generates from the claim ledger rather than from direct text edits. Under the behavior order in Section 4 and Section 6, closing reconciliation runs after review and adjudication finish, narrows C40 to what the text states, and drops C48 because the manuscript does not state it.

F1-citations-2 (Did the evaluated run exercise the referee loop?) was settled by gemini: adopt_author. The author's last answer stands because S6 already satisfies the requested manuscript changes and Galley updates the claim ledger at closing reconciliation rather than through direct edits to Appendix A. Across all three rounds, the referee confirms that S6 separates configured settings from completed activity and presents answer judgment and adjudication as implemented mechanisms. S6 states only the configured cap of three answers per finding and the configured limit of two referee rounds, while S9 reports the run counts from the production record. The referee's remaining objection concerns C11 in Appendix A, which still states that the run used two referee rounds. Galley generates Appendix A from the claim ledger at typesetting and does not accept direct text edits to that appendix. Under the ladder in S4 and the closing check in S6, the reconcile behavior runs after peer review under a family other than the author's and narrows C11 to match the revised text before the typeset behavior regenerates Appendix A. Finally, although the referee disputes a remark in the author's rebuttal about whether a round formally closed, S6 makes no claim that a round closed.

F1-methods-5 (How were defects and controls selected, how were their expected labels established, and how did a narrower judgment count?) was settled by gemini: narrow. Both sides are partly right. What is not known from the material in this request is how calibrate selects controls from the verified citations, how it constructs planted defects, and how it scores narrower judgments toward the two calibration rates; stating those rules in prose would invent facts, while Section 7 already limits both rates to this run's planted set and distinguishes control consistency from independently established accuracy, and Section 9 and the Abstract report the case counts (6 of 6 planted defects and 2 of 2 controls). At the same time, the referee is right that Section 7 overreaches by stating that every control was already judged supported, because Section 5 and Claim C34 allow verified citations to be accepted under either supported or narrower judgments, and Section 7's reference to calibrate in Galley's source omitted control selection and the verifier's three-way judgment, including narrower judgments, while leaving Galley's uncapitalized. The edits narrow Section 7 to state that controls were accepted during verification and that calibrate in Galley's source defines control selection, planted-defect construction, and how all three verifier judgments, including narrower judgments, count toward the two rates.

F1-citations-8 (What are the seven factors, and where did the rubric come from?) was settled by gemini: adopt_author. Rounds 1 and 2 resolved the attribution and validity issues raised by the citations referee. S5 identifies the seven-factor rubric as the authors' own design heuristic rather than an external standard, states its input-to-verdict procedure as a non-blocking improver (worth writing, reformulate, or no contribution), and S10 leaves predictive validity open as an untested hypothesis. Neither the thesis, any load-bearing claim, nor any result reported in S9 depends on the individual factor names, factor-level scoring criteria, or score-to-verdict mapping rule; the governed cross-family decision in S5 is direction selection after a reformulate verdict, and other non-load-bearing improvers such as reassess and fidelity are specified at the same input-to-verdict level. Moreover, the seed, claim ledger, and production record in the request do not specify the seven factor names, scoring criteria, or verdict mapping rule. Supplying them would invent details absent from the record, whereas stating in the prose that the manuscript omits them would comment on what the text documents rather than state a limitation of the work itself.

F1-citations-5 (Which citation pathway is subject to the abstract-only gate?) was settled by gemini: adopt_referee. The referee is right that the manuscript still states the verbatim abstract gate without scope outside S5. S5 distinguishes claim-level abstract matching from systematic-review full-text auditing, whereas the abstract, S1 and S7 still describe verbatim abstract matching without restricting it to citations from claim-level evidence search, and S5's second verification paragraph leaves 'each such citation' immediately after the sentence on systematic reviews. The edits restrict the verbatim abstract gate to citations from claim-level evidence search across the abstract, S1, S5 and S7. Appendix A (including C34) is generated from the claim ledger rather than edited directly, and closing reconciliation aligns C34 with the scoped manuscript text.

F1-citations-9 (Where can a reader inspect the literature index and the retrieval component used by Galley?) was settled by gemini: adopt_author. Section 5 already cites OpenAlex [@priem2022openalex; @priem2024openalex] where it first names the index and identifies Galley's MIT-licensed repository at https://github.com/autonomio/galley as containing Galley's source, including its calls to Canary. The material in this request gives no separate URL, repository, license or citation for Canary's own retrieval and systematic-review implementation, so the location of Canary's own code is not known from the record. Adopting the referee's demand would invent a source location, stating that Canary is unreleased would invent an unsupported fact about the software, and noting that the manuscript omits a Canary link would comment on what the text documents rather than state a limitation of the work itself. Section 5 does not claim that the Galley repository contains Canary's implementation, and accepted citations can be checked against their cited works through the passages and sources recorded in the claim ledger and the Resolvent evidence package. The author's last answer stands with no edits.

summary: Galley presents a concrete governance mechanism for scholarly writing and demonstrates the workflow on one seed. I would hold the manuscript before review because its claim ledger contradicts the paper’s central reconciliation claim and the evaluation gives readers no trace with which to check that claim.

Galley documents a seed-to-preprint workflow with code-enforced separation of duties and a claim-level evidence trail, exercised in one unattended run. The preprint needs a reconciled provenance record, a clearer comparison with related scholarly tools, and reliability claims that match the checks performed.

Most verified citations match their quoted OpenAlex abstract passages after the earlier revisions, but load-bearing claim C32 in Section 2 asserts that LLM-generated scholarly text contains misattributed citations on the basis of two snippet passages that mention neither language models nor scholarly text, while Section 1 newly overreaches a secondary summary of individual-model self-preference to claim that developer-family review is non-independent. In addition, Section 2 and Section 8 split a single fault-seeding caveat as if it were a separate dissenting study, leave the Resolvent format uncited, and omit foundational priority work expected by digital-libraries and AI-writing readers across multi-family evaluation juries, end-to-end manuscript generation, abstract-level scientific claim verification, role-based separation of duties, and claim-level scholarly provenance.

The manuscript presents a coherent architectural design for cross-family separation of duties and in-run diagnostic checks in semi-autonomous scholarly editing, and most claims align with the system specification and verified abstract passages. However, material scoping and reporting gaps remain—including misreporting the number of claims lacking external evidence in Section 9, omitting the absence of independent human ground-truth auditing and three-family seat reuse across stages in Sections 3 and 10, overstating reconciliation, calibration, family-bias, and replay scope in Sections 1, 6, and 7, and leaving a seat-assignment collision in Section 11's proposed factorial study—all of which can be resolved through targeted prose revisions.

text: F2-field-1 (Why does the claim ledger retain a load-bearing novelty claim that the manuscript withdrew for lack of evidence?) was settled by gemini: adopt_author. The author's rebuttal stands because the manuscript body already excludes the disputed claims and the claim ledger updates only during post-review reconciliation. Neither the title, the abstract nor Sections 1–11 state C40's comparison with the closest prior systems or the unverified hypotheses in C29, C46 and C48, as the referee acknowledges in Round 3. Typesetting generates Appendix A from the claim ledger rather than from direct text edits, so manuscript edits cannot alter those ledger entries. Under the behavior ladder in Section 4 and the reconciliation design in Section 6, reconcile (behavior 24) and typeset (behavior 26) run after referee, respond, verify-disposition and adjudicate (behaviors 19–23) finish. During review and adjudication, Appendix A therefore shows the pre-reconciliation ledger, and its gaps against the reviewed body text provide the input that reconcile corrects once review closes. Cross-family separation of duties in Section 3 assigns ledger reconciliation to a model family other than the author's after review ends, and Section 9 states the finished manuscript's properties rather than narrating an intermediate production stage.

F2-field-2 (What establishes agreement across the final artifacts when the supplied ledger contradicts the manuscript on recorded claims?) was settled by gemini: narrow. Both seats are partly right. The author is right that in Galley's 27-step ladder, reconciliation runs at step 24 after peer review and adjudication (steps 19-23) finish, code forbids the author's family from reconciling its own claims, and Appendix A is generated from the claim ledger at typesetting rather than edited directly; pre-reconciliation discrepancies such as C40, C29 and C48 and the unavailability of reconciled companion files during review follow from that order. The referee is right that Sections 6 and 8 still state post-reconciliation agreement with the manuscript prose as an unconditional guarantee, conflate single-revision derivation of claim entries across the three rendered outputs with prose-to-ledger verification, and omit from the evaluation limitations that alignment of the reconciled artifacts with the final text went unverified. The edits narrow Sections 6 and 8 so claim-to-text alignment on recorded claims rests explicitly on the reconciling family's judgment while single-revision typesetting aligns claim entries across the appended ledger, evidence package and sign-off sheet after review ends, and state once in Section 10 that no person verified that those reconciled artifacts match the final text.

F2-field-7 (What makes the automated workflow a systematic review whose search, screening, and findings another team could audit?) was settled by gemini: adopt_referee. The referee is right that the documented workflow supports finding-level verification against quoted full-text passages and an independent model audit rather than an auditable systematic review, and that the manuscript must use one term consistently. Section 5 already defines the workflow as a "model-run review" and states its finding-level audit grain, whereas Sections 3 and 10 still retain "systematic review". Replacing "systematic review" with "model-run review" in Section 3 (with a cross-reference to Section 5) and in both occurrences in Section 10 unifies the term across all editable manuscript sections, from which closing reconciliation updates ledger claims C7 and C42 (Appendix A is generated from the claim ledger and is not edited directly).

F2-editor-1 (How can this run demonstrate reconciliation when its published ledger still contains claims that contradict or exceed the final text?) was settled by gemini: narrow. Both sides are partly right. The author is right on execution order, separation of duties and available data: reconcile (step 24) runs only after referee review, responses, judgments and adjudication (steps 19–23) settle; Appendix A is generated from the claim ledger at typesetting rather than edited directly; the author family cannot edit ledger standings without judging its own claims; companion artifacts are derived from the same state at typesetting rather than compared separately; and post-reconciliation counts cannot be invented before step 24 runs. However, the referee is right that the manuscript prose currently overclaims what reconciliation and the self-referential evaluation establish: Sections 6 and 8 assert unconditionally that after reconciliation the ledger, evidence package and sign-off sheet say what the manuscript says, even though reconciliation is an uncalibrated, unaudited model judgment on recorded claims; Abstract and Section 9 attribute pre-reconciliation ledger counts (45 claims, 27 system-added claims, 5 unsupported claims stated as hypotheses) to the reconciled final argument and report 9 narrowed claims without identifying that those narrowings occurred during citation verification; and Section 10 omits closing reconciliation and companion artifacts from its list of unaudited outputs. The edits narrow Sections 6, 8, 9, 10 and the Abstract to that common ground.

Final profile: input_not_output 2/3, shared_bottleneck 2/3, conventional_body_one_graft 2/3, surprising_and_certain 0/3, opens_more_than_closes 2/3, cheap_to_adopt 2/3, early 2/3. Weakest: surprising_and_certain. Compared with the pre-drafting seed (2, 1, 1, 0, 2, 1, 2), the finished manuscript raises shared_bottleneck, conventional_body_one_graft, and cheap_to_adopt from 1 to 2 by recentring on citation fabrication and evaluator self-preference, grounding Related Work in 23 verified OpenAlex citations across five literature streams, and extracting a standalone three-family governance pattern alongside an MIT-licensed codebase. However, surprising_and_certain remains at 0—and under a multiplicative standard where one near-zero factor sinks a paper, the manuscript should be reformulated rather than sent out as-is. To stay faithful to its evidence, the run narrowed its thesis to a tautological internal existence claim ('submission-ready under its own gates' on one self-referential seed with no baseline and no human audit), where 26 of 44 ledger claims needed no external evidence as the authors' own work or premises, 4 of 18 external claims (including the core gap claim C29) ended as unverified hypotheses, and calibration checked only 6 planted defects and 2 previously accepted controls. Reframing the paper around the controlled 3x3 cross-family versus single-family replay experiment proposed in Section 11—evaluated on external seeds with blinded human audits while trimming residual science-of-science and system-tour sprawl—is needed to convert an honest architectural demonstration into a surprising, certain empirical contribution.
